draft.title: Status, power and culture
card: Status
a person's standing or rank in a group, based on things such as role, success or respect. People often pay more attention to high-status people and are more likely to copy them.
Power
the ability to control or affect what others do, for example by giving rewards, setting rules or applying penalties. A person with power can often get others to act as they ask.
Culture
the shared beliefs, values and customs of a group. Cultural norms are the unwritten rules about how to act, such as how to greet an elder or speak to a leader.

These three work together. Norms in a culture can decide who is treated as high status, and how much people defer to those with power. The same person may be treated differently in different cultures.
draft.remember: Status, power and cultural norms all shape how people treat someone and how much influence that person has.

a.q: Why might a team of junior players copy the habits of the club captain?
opts: The captain has high status in the group
The captain has less influence than other players
The captain is the same age as the juniors
The juniors are copying the group's smallest member
a.why: The captain's role gives them high status, so others pay attention to them and tend to follow their lead. Age does not explain it, because the card links influence to standing in the group.
a.clue: Think about the captain's standing in the team.

b.q: Priya moves from a school where students speak freely to teachers, to a school where a cultural norm is to stand and wait for a teacher to speak first. What best explains why students there wait to be addressed?
opts: A cultural norm shapes how people act toward authority
Students there have more status than their teachers
The teachers at that school have less power than others
Students there are copying the newest student's habits
b.why: A norm is an unwritten rule about how to act, and this one guides how students treat a person with authority. Giving teachers less power or students more status would not lead to waiting to be addressed.
b.clue: Look for the unwritten rule about how to act.

a.best: The captain has high status in the group

b.best: A cultural norm shapes how people act toward authority

b.q: Priya moves to a new school where students stand and wait for a teacher to speak first. There is no school rule about it, and nobody is punished for speaking first. What best explains why students wait?
opts: Shared customs shape how students treat teachers
Teachers use penalties to make students wait
A school rule requires students to wait silently
Students there have higher status than teachers
b.why: With no rule and no penalty, the waiting comes from the group's shared customs, which are cultural norms about how to treat people in authority. Penalties are tempting because power can change behaviour, but the scenario says nobody is punished.
b.clue: If nobody enforces it, where does the expectation come from?
